151.question: Which display mode of a string control lets you see and edit non-printable characters (such as line feeds or tabs) using sequences like '\n' and '\t'?

options.a: '\ Codes Display'
options.b: 'Password Display'
options.c: 'Hex Display'
options.d: 'Normal Display'

151.explanation: The string control's '\ Codes Display' mode shows non-printable characters as readable escape sequences (for example, \n for a line feed), which is useful for debugging.

152.question: Which display mode of a string control/indicator is appropriate for showing binary content in hexadecimal format, for example when communicating with instruments that send raw data?

options.a: 'Hex Display'
options.b: 'Password Display'
options.c: 'Normal Display'
options.d: '\ Codes Display'

152.explanation: 'Hex Display' mode shows each byte of the string as its hexadecimal representation, useful for inspecting raw binary data received from instruments or protocols.

153.question: What is a string literal (string constant) on the block diagram, and what color is its border drawn in?

options.a: A fixed text constant, shown with a pink/magenta border, matching the color of the string data type
options.b: A function that converts Booleans to text
options.c: A type of conditional control structure
options.d: A mandatory global variable

153.explanation: Like string wires, string constants have a pink/magenta border, visually identifying their data type.

154.question: Format Into String is used with the format string '%d degrees %s' and an integer value (25) and a string ('Celsius') are wired to it. What would the expected result be?

options.a: '25 degrees Celsius'
options.b: '%d degrees %s'
options.c: A run-time error due to incompatible types
options.d: 'degrees Celsius 25'

154.explanation: The %d specifier inserts the integer value formatted as a decimal and %s inserts the string as-is, respecting the order of the wired inputs: the result combines both values within the fixed text.

155.question: Which operation is most appropriate for checking whether a string contains a specific substring at any position, without needing to know its exact location?

options.a: Use Match Pattern or Search and Replace String to detect the presence of the pattern
options.b: Use String Length exclusively
options.c: Use Build Array
options.d: Use Bundle by Name

155.explanation: Match Pattern (or equivalent search functions) lets you determine whether a pattern/substring exists within a string, regardless of its exact position.

156.question: Which function converts a Boolean value into its string representation (for example 'TRUE' or 'FALSE')?

options.a: Boolean to String (or Format Into String with %s applied after conversion)
options.b: Number to String
options.c: String Length
options.d: Match Pattern

156.explanation: LabVIEW offers specific conversion functions, such as Boolean to String, for turning a Boolean value into its equivalent textual representation.

157.question: Why is it important to distinguish between the String data type and the Path data type in LabVIEW, even though both can display similar text?

options.a: Because Path is its own data type with specific cross-platform formatting rules for file paths, distinct from a generic string
options.b: Because a Path can never be converted to a string
options.c: Because both are exactly the same data type internally
options.d: Because String only accepts uppercase text

157.explanation: Although a Path may visually look like a text string, LabVIEW treats it as an independent data type, with its own cross-platform internal format, and explicit conversion functions are required to go from one to the other.

158.question: What is the main use of the 'Trim Whitespace' function on a string?

options.a: To remove leftover spaces, tabs and line feeds at the start and/or end of the string
options.b: To convert all the text to uppercase
options.c: To count the number of words in the string
options.d: To concatenate two strings, discarding the second

158.explanation: Trim Whitespace removes leftover whitespace characters (spaces, tabs, line feeds) from the ends of a string, useful for cleaning up data read from files or instruments.

159.question: What is a SubVI in LabVIEW?

options.a: A VI used within the block diagram of another VI, working analogously to a subroutine or function
options.b: A VI that can only run once per LabVIEW session
options.c: A type of flow control structure
options.d: A project configuration file

159.explanation: A SubVI is simply a VI called from the block diagram of another VI (the 'parent' VI), reusing its functionality as if it were a subroutine.

160.question: What are the two essential elements a VI must have in order to be used correctly as a SubVI?

options.a: A configured icon and connector pane
options.b: A shift register and a Formula Node
options.c: An array and a cluster
options.d: A Case Structure and a While Loop

160.explanation: For a VI to work as a reusable SubVI, it needs its icon (graphical representation) and its connector pane (which exposes inputs and outputs) defined.

161.question: What general steps are followed to convert a portion of existing block diagram code into a new SubVI?

options.a: Select the desired code and use the 'Create SubVI' option from the Edit menu, which automatically encapsulates the selected code
options.b: Manually copy each function to a blank VI, one by one, with no automatic tool
options.c: Delete the code and rewrite it entirely in a new VI
options.d: Use only the Project Explorer, without touching the block diagram

161.explanation: LabVIEW offers the 'Create SubVI' option (Edit > Create SubVI) which automatically encapsulates the selected code in a new VI, generating its basic icon and connector pane.

162.question: Which element of a SubVI, editable by double-clicking the icon in the upper-right corner of the front panel, lets you customize its graphical appearance?

options.a: The Icon Editor
options.b: The Connector Pane Editor
options.c: VI Properties
options.d: The Project Explorer

162.explanation: The Icon Editor opens by double-clicking the VI's icon and lets you design the graphical representation that will be shown when that VI is used as a SubVI.

163.question: What does the connector pane pattern chosen for a SubVI determine?

options.a: The number and geometric arrangement of input and output terminals available for wiring to the SubVI
options.b: The color of the VI's icon
options.c: The maximum number of times the SubVI can run
options.d: The default data type of all the VI's controls

163.explanation: The connector pane pattern defines how many terminals (and in what arrangement) will be available for assigning controls and indicators as inputs and outputs of the SubVI.

164.question: When configuring the connector pane of a SubVI, how is a front panel control assigned to a specific connector terminal?

options.a: By clicking the desired terminal on the connector pane and then clicking the corresponding control on the front panel
options.b: By dragging the control directly onto the block diagram
options.c: By typing the control's name into the VI's icon
options.d: It happens automatically with no user involvement and no way to choose the terminal

164.explanation: To assign a control to a terminal, you first click the desired terminal within the connector pane (the cursor changes to a wiring spool) and then click the corresponding control or indicator on the front panel.

165.question: What visually distinguishes, on the connector pane, a terminal already assigned to a control from one that has not yet been assigned?

options.a: The assigned terminal shows the color of the corresponding data type, whereas an unassigned one appears white/gray
options.b: There is no visual difference at all between the two states
options.c: The assigned terminal flashes permanently
options.d: The unassigned terminal is hidden automatically

165.explanation: A connector pane terminal takes on the color associated with the data type of the control/indicator assigned to it; unassigned terminals stay white.

166.question: Where do you write the general description of a VI and of each of its controls/indicators, which is then visible in Context Help?

options.a: In the documentation properties of VI Properties and in the Description and Tip window of each control
options.b: In the VI's file name
options.c: In a free comment on the block diagram, only
options.d: In the Project Explorer

166.explanation: The general description is configured in File > VI Properties > Documentation, and that of each individual control/indicator in its properties window (Description and Tip); both are then visible in Context Help.

167.question: What is the 'tip strip' of a control or indicator in LabVIEW?

options.a: A small pop-up text that appears when you hover the cursor over the object, showing a brief description of its purpose
options.b: A toolbar exclusive to the connector pane
options.c: A type of sequence structure
options.d: A mandatory attachment for every VI

167.explanation: The tip strip is a short, configurable piece of text shown as a floating tooltip when the cursor hovers over a control or indicator, helping to quickly document its function.

168.question: What is VI 'reentrancy' in LabVIEW?

options.a: A setting that allows multiple instances of the same VI to run simultaneously, each with its own independent data memory
options.b: A property exclusive to Boolean controls
options.c: A step-by-step debugging mode
options.d: A type of conditional control structure

168.explanation: A reentrant VI allows several simultaneous calls to the same SubVI to run in parallel (for example, from different parallel loops), each keeping its own independent data state.

169.question: By default, when a VI is NOT reentrant and is called simultaneously from two different places in parallel code, what happens?

options.a: One of the calls must wait for the other to finish, since they share the same data memory (non-reentrant behavior)
options.b: Both calls run fully in parallel with no restriction
options.c: LabVIEW generates a compile error when it detects parallel calls
options.d: The VI automatically becomes reentrant for that run

169.explanation: By default VIs are non-reentrant and share a single instance of memory; if they are called in parallel, one call must wait for the previous one to finish before starting, to avoid data conflicts.

170.question: What is one of the main advantages of splitting a large application into several SubVIs instead of one monolithic VI?

options.a: It improves modularity, reuse and maintainability of the code
options.b: It automatically halves the program's execution time
options.c: It completely removes the need to handle errors
options.d: It prevents the code from being debugged

170.explanation: Splitting code into SubVIs favours modularity, allows common functionality to be reused, makes individual testing easier, and improves the readability and overall maintenance of the application.

171.question: Which action lets you quickly open the block diagram of a SubVI from the block diagram of the VI that calls it?

options.a: Double-click the SubVI's icon
options.b: Right-click and select 'Delete'
options.c: Press Ctrl+R
options.d: Drag the icon off the diagram

171.explanation: Double-clicking a SubVI's icon on the block diagram makes LabVIEW automatically open its front panel (from which its block diagram can be reached).

172.question: Which standard connector pane geometric pattern is recommended when a SubVI has only 2 inputs and 2 outputs?

options.a: A simple 4-terminal pattern (2x2)
options.b: Always the 28-terminal pattern, regardless of how many are used
options.c: A pattern with a single terminal only
options.d: There is no need to choose a pattern if the VI has few connections

172.explanation: LabVIEW offers several predefined connector patterns, and it is recommended to choose the one that best fits the actual number of inputs/outputs, avoiding unnecessarily large patterns such as the 28-terminal one.

173.question: What happens if a terminal on a SubVI's connector pane is left unassigned to any control or indicator?

options.a: That terminal is simply not available as a usable input/output when the SubVI is called
options.b: The VI cannot be saved until all terminals are assigned
options.c: LabVIEW automatically assigns a random value to that terminal
options.d: The SubVI can no longer run independently

173.explanation: An unassigned terminal on the connector pane simply stays inactive; it does not appear as an available input or output when that VI is used as a SubVI, although the VI can be saved and run normally.

174.question: Which aspect of a SubVI's icon helps the user visually identify its function within a complex block diagram, without having to open it?

options.a: A graphical design and/or descriptive text inside the icon
options.b: The file name, which is always hidden in the icon
options.c: The background color of the front panel
options.d: The number of Boolean controls in the VI

174.explanation: A well-designed icon, with symbols or text representing the SubVI's function, makes it easy to quickly identify its purpose within large block diagrams.

175.question: A non-reentrant SubVI performs a calculation that takes 2 seconds. This SubVI is called twice in parallel from two independent branches of the main VI's block diagram. What is the approximate total execution time of both calls combined?

options.a: Approximately 4 seconds, since the calls are serialized because they share the same memory instance
options.b: Approximately 2 seconds, because both calls run in parallel without restriction
options.c: Approximately 1 second, because LabVIEW automatically splits the load between the two calls
options.d: It is indeterminate and depends solely on the hardware, unrelated to reentrancy

175.explanation: Because it is not reentrant, both calls share the same data memory, so one must wait for the other to finish; the approximate total time is the sum of both executions (2+2=4 seconds).
